Weight Features by the Candidate Models That Use Them

Source: R/formula_sampling.R
calculate_feature_weights.Rd

Turns a set of scored candidate formulas into one weight per feature: how much of the total model score sits in the formulas that contain the feature. Use it to learn, in a training fold, which predictors to favour when sampling the next round of candidates ([sample_candidate_formulas()] `weights`).

Usage

calculate_feature_weights(
  candidates,
  scores = NULL,
  method = c("score", "inclusion"),
  higher_is_better = TRUE,
  level = c("variable", "term"),
  normalize = c("none", "sum", "max")
)

Arguments

candidates

A tibble from [sample_candidate_formulas()], or a list of formulas or of character vectors of terms.

scores

Numeric vector, one score per candidate (needed unless `method = "inclusion"`). Candidates with an `NA` score are dropped, with a warning.

method

`"score"` (default) or `"inclusion"`.

higher_is_better

Logical; set `FALSE` for losses such as the Brier score.

level

`"variable"` (default) or `"term"`.

normalize

`"none"` (default), `"sum"` or `"max"`.

Value

A tibble with `feature`, `weight`, `n_formulas` (how many formulas contain it) and `rank`, ordered by weight (ties by name).

Definition

Each formula gets a share `s_i` of the total score: scores are shifted so the worst is 0 (`score - min(score)`, after flipping the sign when `higher_is_better = FALSE`) and divided by their sum; if all scores are equal every formula gets `1 / n`. The weight of a feature is the sum of the shares of the formulas that contain it, a number between 0 and 1: 1 means it is in every formula that scores above the worst, 0 that it is in none. Because the worst candidate always gets a share of 0, a feature found only in the worst formula gets weight 0, and a tiny score gap can swing weights between 0 and 1; if you pass these weights to [sample_candidate_formulas()] a 0 keeps the term out of the next round, so add a small constant to the weights if you want every term to stay possible. `method = "inclusion"` ignores the scores and gives the plain fraction of formulas that contain the feature. `normalize = "sum"` rescales the weights to add to 1 and `"max"` rescales the largest to 1.

What counts as a feature

With `level = "variable"` (default) a feature is a variable: `log(x)` and `poly(x, 2)` count for `x`, an interaction `a:b` counts for both `a` and `b`, and a variable counts once per formula however many terms use it. With `level = "term"` a feature is a whole term as written (`"log(x)"`, `"a:b"`).

Data boundaries

The function only sees formulas and their scores. The scores must be computed on the **training** rows of the fold you are in (for example by an inner cross-validation inside the training set); a score computed on the held-out rows would leak them into the weights.

See also

[sample_candidate_formulas()]

Examples

cand <- sample_candidate_formulas(c("age", "sex", "bmi", "lactate"), n = 8, max_size = 3, seed = 2)
scores <- c(0.61, 0.70, 0.66, 0.72, 0.58, 0.69, 0.64, 0.71)[seq_len(nrow(cand))]
calculate_feature_weights(cand, scores)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   feature weight n_formulas  rank
#>   <chr>    <dbl>      <int> <int>
#> 1 age      0.672          5     1
#> 2 sex      0.463          4     2
#> 3 bmi      0.418          3     3
#> 4 lactate  0.358          3     4
